case_name: DCP v. A.D.D., J.D. and B.J.T.
text:
SUPREME
COURT OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

Citation:
DCP
v. A.D.D., J.D. and B.J.T.
, 2020 PESC 23

Date: 20200602

Docket:
S1FS9016

Registry:
Charlottetown

Between:

The
Director of Child Protection for

the
Province of Prince Edward Island

Applicant

And:

A.D.D.,
J.D., and B.J.T.

Respondents

Before:
The Honourable Justice Nancy L. Key

Appearances:

David Larter,
solicitor for the Applicant

Chris Montigny,
Amicus
Curiae

A.D.D. not present
and not represented

Sophie MacDonald, solicitor
for J.D.

Ryan Moss,
solicitor for B.J.T.

Place
and dates of hearing                           -                            February
24, 25, and 26, 2020

Charlottetown,
Prince Edward Island

Place and date of
oral submissions                        -
March 11, 2020

Charlottetown,
Prince Edward Island

Place
and date of written decision              -
June 2, 2020

Charlottetown,
Prince Edward Island

HEADNOTE:
Disposition Hearing – the court previously found child in need of protection
from his mother A.D.D.; Director of Child Protection has no protection concerns
about father or maternal grandmother of child; mother unable to put forward a
plan of care; after considering the best interests of the child the court ordered
the child to be returned to his maternal grandmother.

STATUTES
CONSIDERED:
Child
Protection Act
,

S.P.E.I.
2000 (2
nd
) Cap. C-5.1

STATUTUES REFERRED
TO:
Custody,
Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act,
R.S.P.E.I 1988, Cap. C-3

CASES CONSIDERED:
DCP v. A.D.D.,
J.D. and B.J.T.
,

2020 PESC 9
(CanLII)
;

DCW (PEI) v. A.H. and J.D.
,
2009 PECA 19
;
Nova Scotia
(Community Services) v. T. H.
,

2010 NSCA 63 (CanLII)
;
Hryniak
v. Mauldin
,
2014 SCC 7 (CanLII)
;

DCP v. S.M. &
W.D.
,

2010 PESC 41 (CanLII)

RULES CONSIDERED:

Prince
Edward Island Rules of Civil Procedure
, Rule 53.03(3),

Key, J.
:

Background:

[
1
]

The review hearing on this matter took place in January, 2020. By
decision filed February 11, 2020, (
DCP v. A.D.D., J.D. and B.J.T.
,

2020 PESC 9 (CanLII)
), I  determined that W.F.D. (W.D.) born October 15, 2013
continued to be a child in need of protection pursuant to s. 9(p) of the
Child
Protection Act
,

S.P.E.I. 2000 (2
nd
) Cap.
C-5.1 (the
Act
).

[
2
]

Section 9(p) of the
Act
states:

9.
…

(p)                    the child suffers from a mental, emotional or developmental condition  that, if not
addressed, could seriously harm the child and the parent does not or refuses to
obtain treatment or is
unavailable or unable to consent to services or
treatment to remedy or ameliorate the effects of the condition;
…

(my
emphasis)

[
3
]

W.D. was determined to be in need of protection from his mother,
A.D.­D. (A.D.D.)
at that time
.

[
4
]

In a decision dated July 2, 2019 the Court ordered that W.D.’s
maternal grandmother, B.J.T. (B.J.T.) is a parent pursuant to s.1(s) of the
Act
.
Therefore, for the purposes of the
Act
, both J.D. and B.J.T. are
parents. Additionally, the order included the appointment of an
Amicus
Curiae
on specific terms. The
Amicus
, Mr. Montigny, participated in both
the protection and disposition hearings.

[
5
]

Just prior to the review hearing the Director
advised there were no protection concerns in relation to W.D.’s father, J.D.
(J.D.) or his grandmother B.J.T.

[
6
]

W.D., age 4 at the time of apprehension, is on the Autism
Spectrum but is high functioning. A detailed timeline of the involvement of the
Director of Child Protection (the Director) with this family is set out in my
earlier decision:

[14]   Certain facts were provided by the
Amicus
,
Mr. Montigny in his factum. All counsel agreed that, for the purpose of Mr.
Montigny’s motion, the facts were correct.

1.

[W.D.], born October 15, 2013 (hereinafter “
[W.D.]
”) is the son
of the Respondent [A.D.D.] (hereinafter “
[A.D.D.]
”) and the Respondent
[J.D.] (hereinafter “
[J.D.]
”). The Respondent [B.J.T.] is [A.D.D.]’s
mother and [W.D.]’s grandmother.

2.

[W.D.] was apprehended by the Applicant, the Director of Child
Protection for the Province of Prince Edward Island (hereinafter the “
Director
”)
on January 16, 2018. [W.D.] was four years of age.

3.

[W.D.] was apprehended from the care of [A.D.D.] pursuant to
the
Child Protection Act,
S.P.E.I. 2000 (2
nd
) Cap. C-5.1
(hereinafter the “
Act
”). On January 16, 2018, both [A.D.D.] and [W.D.]
were residing in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.

4.

On January 16, 2018, [J.D.] was residing in Alberta and did not
have custody of or visitation with [W.D].

5.

[W.D.] was apprehended without a court order. Pursuant to section
27(1)(b) of the Act, the Director had four clear days to apply for an order
under section 29. The Director filed a Notice of Application on January 22,
2018.

6.

The matter was set for an interim hearing pursuant to section 31 of the
Act for January 25, 2018 in front of Justice Gormley. The matter was adjourned
at the request of [A.D.D.] (via her then legal counsel).

7.

The interim hearing pursuant to section 31 of
the Act was held on February 8, 2018 in front of Justice Key. The Court found
there was a
prima facie
case that [W.D.] was a child in need of
protection and a protection hearing pursuant to section 36 of the Act was
ordered.

8.

A protection hearing pursuant to section 36 of the Act was
scheduled to be heard on March 15, 2018 in front of Justice Gormley. The hearing
did not proceed and the matter was adjourned to April 23, 2018.

9.

A combined protection and disposition hearing was held by Justice
Matheson between April 23-25, 2018. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Court
took the matter under advisement.

10.

On May 29, 2018, Justice Matheson rendered the decision of the
Court finding that [W.D.] was a child in need of protection and, pursuant to
section 38 of the Act, ordered that subject to specified terms that [W.D.]
remain in the temporary care of the Director for a period of three months.

11.

The court order expired on August 29, 2018. On August 28, 2018 the Director filed a
Notice of Application for a review of the May 29, 2018 disposition order.

12.

The Review Hearing pursuant to section 39 was
scheduled for October 3, 2018 in front of Justice Cheverie. It was scheduled to
resume on November 28, 2018. The Court does not hear any evidence at the
October 3, 2018 hearing.

13.

January 16, 2019 was the one year anniversary of [W.D.] having
been apprehended.

14.

May 29, 2019 was the one year anniversary of Justice Matheson’s
protection and disposition decision.

15.

The review hearing is scheduled for January 13, 2020.

16.

[W.D.] remains in the custody and guardianship of the Director
pursuant to the [May] 29, 2018 Order of Justice Matheson.

[
7
]

As noted, W.D. was apprehended on January 16, 2018. He continues
to remain in the custody and guardianship of the Director notwithstanding the
review hearing took place approximately 20 months after he was apprehended,
well beyond the statutorily mandated time limits set out in the
Act
.

[
8
]

Pursuant to a foster care placement, W.D. resided with his
grandmother B.J.T. for approximately 12 months. With no notice and for flimsy
reasons, the Director removed W.D. from his grandmother B.J.T.’s care, placed
him in foster care for approximately 4 weeks and then removed him from the
province of Prince Edward Island in early August, 2019. He was placed with his
father J.D. in Calgary, Alberta. Although sent to Alberta for a visit, W.D. has
resided there ever since.

[
9
]

The court made the finding of protection as against A.D.D. as a
result of expert evidence indicating that A.D.D. has schizophrenia, (a lifelong
brain based disorder), Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and depression. The
totality of the evidence before the court was sufficiently compelling to
require a finding that W.D. continued to be in need of protection because, “…
his mother will not be able to consent, willingly or unwillingly, to services
or treatment for what is a lifelong challenge for [W.D.]” (para. 139). The
court also found that A.D.D. was not, at that time, taking any steps to start
what will be a long term treatment plan. Nor, does it appear, she has done so
since.

[
10
]

In accordance with s. 37 of the
Act

all parties to the proceeding were to file a plan of care. Both J.D. and B.J.T.
filed plans of care. The Director filed no plan of care. From the moment W.D.
was declared a child in need of protection from his mother, the Director
purported to take no position as to whether the court placed W.D. with this
father J.D. or his grandmother B.J.T.

[
11
]

From at least early January onward there have
been no protection concerns about either J.D. or B.J.T. Therefore, what was
placed before the court was a custody battle disguised as a disposition
hearing. Neither J.D. nor B.J.T. has commenced parallel proceedings to
determine the custody of or access to W.D. under the
Custody,
Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act
,

R.S.P.E.I 1988, Cap.
C-3
.

[
12
]

A.D.D. was unable to put forward a plan of care. As the court
noted in its earlier decision, A.D.D. refused to participate in the review
hearing; nor did A.D.D. participate in the disposition hearing. The
Amicus
Curiae
was unable to elicit from A.D.D. any plan of care she might wish to
put forward.

Preliminary Matter:

[
13
]

My earlier decision also held that once the court found W.D. to
be a child in need of protection it had only two options in making a
disposition order. In accordance with section 38 (2) of the
Act
, the
court was required to place the child in the permanent custody and guardianship
of the Director (38(2)(d)) or place the child in the permanent custody and
guardianship of a parent. (38(2)(e)). As noted, the Director did not request
that W.D. be placed in her care.

[
14
]

During his final submissions, counsel for the Director put
another option before the court. He submitted the court may make an order under
s. 38(2)(a) which states:

38.
…

Disposition
order

(2)             …

(a)        that
the child remain with or be placed in the custody of a parent of the child,
subject to the supervision of the Director, for a period not exceeding 6
months; …

[
15
]

I disagree. Section 38(2) sets out the options for the court. It
is apparent from the wording of the section that a placement with a parent
under the supervision of the Director, known as a supervision order, is one
which is temporary in nature. From a practical point of view, if the court were
to make a supervision order, it will end after the maximum six month period and
no order will thereafter remain in place. At that time, a possible scenario
will be for W.D.’s mother to be able to demand the child be returned to her
care since no order would prevent her from doing so.

[
16
]

I am supported in this viewpoint by the comments
of Jenkins, CJ in

DCW (PEI) v. A.H. and J.D.
,
2009 PECA 19
. At
paragraph 19 he states:

19 … The
Act
gives the court a range
of dispositions – from the least interventionalist [sic] of the child being
placed with a parent, through placement with a parent under Director
supervision, to a hybrid of the child being placed in the guardianship of the
Director and returned to a parent upon fulfillment of conditions, to the more
interventionalist  [sic] disposition of placement with the Director
temporarily, and the most interventionalist [sic] of placement in the permanent
custody and guardianship of the Director (
Act
, s. 38(2))...

[
17
]

The range of dispositions including “… the child
being placed with a parent under Director supervision” is a temporary measure.
This disposition includes some involvement by the Director which ends at a
specific time.

[
18
]

I have also reviewed the decision of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in
the case known as
Nova Scotia (Community Services) v. T. H.
,

2010 NSCA 63 (CanLII)
. The Nova Scotia legislation is similar but not
identical. At paragraphs 32 and 47 the court refers to the non-permanent nature
of a supervision order.

[32]       Section
43(1) provides that, in a disposition order involving mere Agency supervision
(i.e. not permanent care and custody of the Agency), the "court may impose
reasonable terms and conditions relating to the child's care and
supervision"…

[47]       I
said earlier that s. 45(1) states maximum time limits for temporary care and
supervision, after which the options are either permanent care and custody
[with or without access under s. 47(2)] or return of the children to the parent…

[
19
]

I agree. In conclusion the option of an order for supervision for
a period not exceeding six months is not available to the court.

[
20
]

Therefore, the sole issue before the court, after considering the
best interests of W.D., is whether W.D. shall be placed in the permanent custody
of his father, J.D. or the permanent custody of his grandmother, B.J.T.

J.D.’s Position:

[
21
]

J.D. is 45 years old and lives in Calgary, Alberta. He has a Bachelor
and Master’s Degree and is steadily employed. He earns additional income from
his passion tying trout flies and has published articles and taught classes in
fly fishing and fly-tying. He resides in a two bedroom townhouse and lives
approximately 20 minutes away from his retired parents. The townhouse is in an
area where there are other children. A school for W.D. is a five minute drive from
J.D.’s home.

[
22
]

J.D. has a sister and niece who reside outside of Canada. He says he is close
to them and sees them whenever possible.

[
23
]

J.D. met W.D. for the first time in late June, 2019. He had no knowledge
of his existence until February, 2019. According to J.D. there are many
resources available in Calgary for children such as W.D.

[
24
]

J.D. is also on the Autism Spectrum. He has spoken at conferences on the
disorder. When his parenting plan was filed on June 18, 2019, he was taking an
eight module parenting course to prepare himself for the time he would be
spending with W.D.

[
25
]

J.D. very much wishes to have W.D. continue to reside with him in
Calgary. He has put forward numerous goals for W.D.’s education, health and
well-being.

B.J.T.’s Position:

[
26
]

B.J.T. is W.D.’s maternal grandmother. She is 65 year old and lives in
Charlottetown, PEI. She has been divorced from A.D.D.’s father for a number of
years and for a period of time A.D.D. and J.D. resided with B.J.T. in Calgary.

[
27
]

When A.D.D. moved to PEI she found she was not able to look after W.D. In
early 2014, B.J.T., then age approximately 58, moved home to PEI to assist her.
From a very early age, W.D. was parented by both A.D.D. and B.J.T. She parented
W.D. for approximately 2 years prior to the Director’s involvement in late
2017.

[
28
]

B.J.T. continues to be employed outside the home. She lives in the same
home W.D. resided in for approximately 12 months prior to being taken to
Calgary. W.D.’s brother, H.B., also lives in Charlottetown and has a good
relationship with his grandmother. H.B. is A.D.D.’s 17 year old son by another
father.

[
29
]

Essentially B.J.T.’s position is to place W.D. back into the same
routine he had prior to being removed from her home with the medical
specialists and other service providers who cared for him prior to his removal
from Prince Edward Island.

Director’s witnesses:

[
30
]

The Director presented three witnesses for cross-examination.

Tracee Sano:

[
31
]

Ms. Sano is a level three access worker for a private company called
Worth Resolving Youth & Family Services in Calgary. The Director entered
into an interprovincial agreement with a sister agency, Calgary Area Child
& Family Service (Calgary Family Services) in order to send W.D. to spend
time with his father.  The arrangement ensures, among other things, the
Director retains the custody and guardianship of W.D. Calgary Family Services
hired Ms. Sano’s employer to work with J.D. and W.D. On this file, Ms. Sano
reported to both a worker in Calgary and Kelly Ragin, W.D.’s family service
worker on PEI. Ms. Sano’s supervisor also saw W.D. once per month and attended
pediatric appointments. Ms. Sano’s work commenced August 25, 2019 and she continued
to be involved on a weekly basis with W.D. and J.D. at the time of this
hearing.

[
32
]

Ms. Sano has experience working with children who are on the autism
spectrum, who have experienced trauma and who are living through complex family
dynamics during their involvement with child protection. Further, she gave evidence
that she has visited J.D. and W.D. at J.D.’s home twice per week (two to six
hours per week) and she speaks with J.D. an additional 1-2 times per week on the
phone.  She also attended W.D.’s school meetings.

[
33
]

She agreed that it would have been a traumatic experience for W.D. to
have been moved from his mother’s home, then a group home, then his grandmother’s
home and that he was not mature enough to understand any of what was happening.

[
34
]

By coaching J.D., Ms. Sano’s goal is to assist J.D. in learning to be a
single father, an intuitive and confident parent, and to help W.D. develop
emotionally and physically. Ms. Sano was very clear that W.D. is her client.

[
35
]

W.D. and B.J.T. were to have FaceTime and telephone contact twice per
week. There were struggles at times to have W.D. contact his grandmother but
Ms. Sano agreed that 5-6 year olds can struggle with contact by phone or FaceTime.
In particular, in September and October, W.D. was extremely oppositional when
the calls were to be made. However, once he was on the calls he was fine and
the content of the calls between W.D. and his grandmother was appropriate.
During the phone calls he smiled and listened to his grandmother. FaceTime was
better. At no point did J.D. initiate the calls; Ms. Sano or another worker did
so.

[
36
]

There were times when calls were not able to be made. If contact was
unable to be made Ms. Sano would contact B.J.T. Ms. Sano stated B.J.T. was
always really gracious and very nice about not being able to speak with W.D.

[
37
]

On one call W.D. mentioned his love for H.B. and it was noted that he
has drawn pictures of H.B. and his mother. He also remembered H.B.’s birthday.
He is very good with numbers and remembers them well. On another call W.D. told
B.J.T. he wanted to go to her house forever and did not want to go back to
Calgary.

[
38
]

At one point Ms. Sano discussed with J.D.’s father and mother that they
facilitate the calls between W.D. and B.J.T. In particular, her request was to J.D.’s
father who had a good rapport with W.D. and was able to encourage W.D. to speak
with his grandmother.

[
39
]

J.D.’s father explained that B.J.T. was someone who had really hurt his
family in the past, and while he wanted to be able to do as requested there was
some fear because of past relationships. Neither was J.D. comfortable making
the calls.

[
40
]

Since W.D. moved to Calgary, there have been a number of what she
described as intense conversations between J.D.’s family and Ms. Sano in
relation to past court proceedings, W.D.’s mother and grandmother, and concerns
about the upcoming court proceedings. Each time, while she understood their
need to explain their anxiety, Ms. Sano felt it was important to remove W.D. so
that he was not present to listen to the adult conversations.

[
41
]

Ms. Sano’s contact logs indicated that J.D. did bring up some concerns
about B.J.T. to Ms. Sano. He wondered how someone on legal aid could afford to
bring up a child from age 6 to 18. As well, J.D. and his family said that B.J.T.
hates their family, lied in her affidavit, slandered their family and supported
A.D.D. in her false allegations against J.D.

[
42
]

J.D. has expressed that he wants to be able to
initiate the calls between W.D. and his grandmother. He is hesitant because of
everything that has happened in the past but he does understand that it
is the best way forward.

[
43
]

Ms. Sano’s evidence about W.D., J.D., his parents and B.J.T. show a
remarkable objectivity. In early February, 2020 approximately two weeks prior
to the disposition hearing, the Director paid for B.J.T.’s flight and hotel so
she could visit W.D. He had not seen her, other than FaceTime, for
approximately six months. Ms. Sano met B.J.T. prior to her seeing W.D. J.D.’s
parents transported W.D. to the visit because they did not want J.D. to have
contact with B.J.T.

[
44
]

In her Supplementary Affidavit filed February 24, 2020 Ms. Sano
described the visits in very positive terms. W.D. and B.J.T. were excited to
see each other and B.J.T. watched and played with W.D., responding to all of
his cues. She noted that W.D. told his Nana that he loved her and missed her,
hugged her and held her hands. She described B.J.T. as using an effective and
kind approach to help W.D. regulate his emotions when he became agitated. Ms.
Sano advised that during the visits W.D. was a pleasant, engaged, happy little
boy who transitioned very well back and forth each day between the two people
he loves.

[
45
]

Ms. Sano told the court she saw the strong connection between W.D. and B.J.T.
W.D.’s grandmother was easily able to get him talking. This pleased Ms. Sano
because she knew then that grandmother and grandson were going to have a happy
visit. W.D. was not defiant with B.J.T. even though he had not seen her in a
long time. He was a pleasure to be around and really engaged with B.J.T. Ms.
Sano said she was pleasantly surprised, in a good way, that B.J.T. has an acute
sense of when W.D. is not telling the truth and handled it in a manner which
W.D. understood. It was apparent to her that the two were very connected and
have spent a long time together. She said that B.J.T. is very good with W.D. in
drawing out the truth and with his behaviours. W.D. was on his best behaviour
during the visits. Ms. Sano had no concerns about B.J.T. caring for W.D. but
acknowledged that W.D.’s time with his grandmother, for that weekend, was much
like vacation time.

[
46
]

The Director required B.J.T.’s time with W.D. to be supervised with no
reasons given. Further, the Director limited the visits to public places with a
total of seven hours permitted over three days. B.J.T.’s request to have W.D.
stay overnight with her in her hotel was denied. Thus, after six months B.J.T.
saw W.D. for three hours on Friday, three hours on Saturday and one hour on Sunday,
the day B.J.T. flew back to P.E.I.

[
47
]

At one point B.J.T. did tell W.D. she would see him soon and Ms. Sano
redirected the conversation because she did not know what the planning was for
W.D. Neither was B.J.T. made aware of the Director’s plans. She believed that W.D.
was coming to Prince Edward Island at the time of the disposition hearing.

[
48
]

Ms. Sano explained to J.D., his parents and B.J.T. the concept of
attachment parenting. The idea is that regardless of what is going on in the
adult world, everyone who has ever loved W.D. continues to love him and it is
very important he know that. Ms. Sano further explained that the reasons for
moving a child from one home to foster care and so on are not understood by the
child. Attachment parenting tries to promote W.D.’s ability to attach to anyone
with whom he stays. He does not need to stay attached to any one person, but he
needs to grow up to know that attachment is good, sustainable, and not
fleeting. She referred to this as the “trust in the world” piece. It is
important the various people who form part of W.D.’s life do everything
possible to reassure him everyone loves him and all the people in his life are
good, supportive people. It is very important for W.D. to trust his caregivers
and his family members and to know that his family members trust one another.

[
49
]

On cross-examination by J.D.’s counsel, Ms. Sano
described J.D. as being a consistent, patient, kind parent who has a close
physical relationship with W.D. She stated that J.D. has become more intuitive
as a parent and she has no concerns with J.D.’s parenting if she was not there
to coach him.

Kelly Ragin:

[
50
]

Kelly Ragin is a Child in Care Social Worker. She
became W.D.’s worker in April, 2019 roughly three months prior to W.D. leaving
for Calgary to stay with his father. She has been following up with the workers
in Calgary since the move.

[
51
]

Ms. Ragin advised the court that she and B.J.T.
got along well and W.D. thrived in B.J.T.’s care. She noted she had negative
interactions with A.D.D. and, at times W.D., when asked, did not want to talk
about his mother. She has not heard from A.D.D. since April, 2019.

[
52
]

In her June, 2019 affidavit Ms. Ragin reported
that W.D. has been doing very well at school overall and his school has an
autism consultant. She attended an appointment with W.D. to see Dr. Gaston, a
pediatrician. She noted Dr. Gaston saw a significant positive change in W.D.’s
presentation while in his grandmother’s care. Dr. Gaston noted W.D. benefits
from routine and Ms. Ragin attached to her affidavit his comments from his
April, 2019 examination of W.D.: “I am amazed at [W.D.]’s progress. He seems so
much more settled, more content, more communicative than I have ever seen him
before. I think a great deal of credit goes to his grandmother here”.

[
53
]

The court acknowledges Dr. Gaston did not give
this evidence directly. However, the court accepts the letter of Dr. Gaston pursuant
to s. 34(3)(a) which permits hearsay evidence of the child which the court
considers reliable.

[
54
]

Ms. Ragin also noted that W.D., until June 2019,
saw A.D.D. twice per week with supervision. She noted W.D. speaks about A.D.D.
and going home, about his brother H.B. but she noted that he does not speak about
his father and says that according to his grandmother, W.D. states he does not
have a father.

[
55
]

Ms. Ragin received a lengthy email from B.J.T.
on June 9
th
. The email set out B.J.T.’s concerns about J.D. and was
sent only one week prior to B.J.T. being advised by Judy Langdon that the

The best interests test:

[
197
]

A judge in a disposition hearing must consider not only the plans of
care of each parent but more importantly the best interests of W.D. Section 2
of the
Act
states:

2.              Primary purpose of Act

(1)                         The
primary purpose of this Act is to protect children from harm due to abuse and
neglect, within the context of section 9 and the best interests of the child.

Best
interests of the child

(2)                         The
best interests of the child means the interests that appear, to the Director,
or to a court, to be best for the child under the circumstances, having regard
to all relevant considerations, including

(a)        the
safety of the child;

(b)        the
capacity of a parent to properly discharge parental obligations;

(c)         the physical,
mental and emotional needs of the child, and the appropriate care or treatment
to meet those needs;

(d)        the
physical, mental and emotional level of development of the child;

(e)        the
views of the child, where appropriate;

(f)         a
secure place for the child and the development of a positive relationship as a
member of a family;

(g)        the
love, affection and ties between the child and persons who have had custody of
the child;

(h)        the
love, affection and ties between the child and other persons in the life of the
child;

(i)         the
cultural, racial, linguistic and religious heritage of the child;

(j)         if the
child is aboriginal, the importance of preserving the cultural identity of the
child;

(k)        the
capacity of persons other than a parent to exercise custody rights and duties
respecting a child;

(l)         the
continuity of care for the child and the possible effect of disruption of that
care on the child; and

(m)       the
difference in the concept of time, and the developmental capacity of a child.

2000(2nd),c.3,s.2; 2010,c.28,s.2.

safety of the child;

I wish to return to s. 2(2)(g):

(g)                        the love, affection and ties between the
child and persons who have had custody of the child;

[

]

In a custody dispute a court may find, after a consideration of the
best interests of a child, the parents are more or less equal in their ability
to parent. However, another factor which may be considered is the question of
which of the two parents is most likely to promote, support and nurture the
child’s relationship with the opposite parent. Where there is conflict between
the parents, one or the other may try in a subtle or not so subtle manner to
weaken or diminish the bond between the child and opposing parent. If that is
the case then the court may rightly place the child with the parent whose focus
is the child’s best interests and not his or her own self-interest.

While J.D. and B.J.T. are more or less equal in their ability to

mother A.D.D. This is not in W.D.’s best interests.

Is it within the jurisdiction of this
court to determine the incidents of custody and access?

[
216
]

In their final submissions
Amicus
, J.D.’s counsel and B.J.T.’s
counsel argued strenuously that the court should, once its decision has been
made, set out the terms of the custodial relationship between J.D. and B.J.T.
In fact, in his documentation B.J.T.’s counsel included as an alternative a
joint custodial relationship between J.D. and B.J.T.

[
217
]

There were many good reasons presented. First, certainty for the
parties and W.D.  A final decision which determines where W.D. is going to live
and under what terms he will spend time with the other parent and family
members has the potential of bringing what has been lengthy litigation to an end.
Another hearing and case management of the process will only increase the time
during which W.D.’s life continues in limbo. He needs routine and certainty.

[
218
]

The cost of more litigation is also a factor.

[
219
]

The
Amicus
, Mr. Montigny submitted that determining at this
stage the incidents of custody and access fits within the guidance provided by
the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in
Hryniak v. Mauldin
,

2014 SCC 7 (Canlii)
. His argument seems to be that the principle of efficiency
and proportionality in
Hryniak
can be adapted to this file and
permit the court to step out on a limb and determine what the future parenting
or custodial arrangements will be for W.D.

[
220
]

With respect I disagree.
Hryniak
was a case involving
the use of a summary judgment procedure where a party was asking the court to
make a shift away from a lengthy, expensive and time consuming trial and arrive
at a decision in a more proportionate manner. Justice Karatkasanis’s opinion
was that such a shift is a requirement for the proper functioning of the
judicial system. In effect, the answer to the question of whether the
“Cadillac” version of a trial is needed, depending on the circumstances, may
well be no. The framework within which judges are to work in making that
determination, in my view, does not apply to this proceeding and any attempt to
mold the
Hryniak
principles to fit this situation may well result
in this judge treading so far out on the branch as to venture into troublesome
territory.

[
221
]

Finally, on this issue, the most important reason not to determine W.D.’s
access with a non-custodial parent is A.D.D. herself. The protection hearing
determined that W.D. was a child in need of protection from his mother
at
this time
.  A.D.D. is currently incapable of looking after W.D. However,
that does not mean that in the future she will not be able to do so. Indeed,
the
Act
permits a parent to apply to terminate a permanent order
“on such grounds as the court may consider just”. (s. 45(2)(a)). As was noted
in the protection hearing, A.D.D. did the best she could, given her mental
illness, to look after W.D. The court found that in a number of respects he was
not a child in need of protection from his mother. Up until just before he was
removed from B.J.T.’s care, A.D.D. and W.D. enjoyed one another’s company under
supervision. A.D.D. loves W.D. and W.D. loves A.D.D.

[
222
]

Therefore, for a court to determine, even on an interim basis, what W.D.’s
life will look like on a day to day basis is to ignore A.D.D.’s voice
completely. She is unable to consent nor to offer an opinion. Her refusal to
participate was, in my view, symptomatic of her larger mental health problems.
However, we cannot ignore the bond between mother and son.

[
223
]

Therefore, for the reasons above I will not determine access after
my custody decision. The parties may rest assured the court will do everything
in its power to facilitate and expedite a hearing on the incidents of access if
the two people who love W.D. cannot come to an agreement.
